title: Act IV, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: At his camp near Sardis, Brutus tells Lucilius that Cassius greets him with cold ceremony, like a hot horse that fails under trial. Cassius arrives angry, saying Brutus has wronged him. Brutus stops him from quarreling before their armies and moves the conversation into his tent.

writingPrompts.text: Supported track (work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act IV, Scene II,” how does Shakespeare show Brutus and Cassius at odds? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act IV, Scene II, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Brutus and Cassius at odds? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the conflict in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act IV, Scene II develops the idea of Brutus and Cassius at odds. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act IV, Scene II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its conflict shape the reader's understanding of Brutus and Cassius at odds. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act IV, Scene II suggests about Brutus and Cassius at odds. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's conflict and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses conflict in Act IV, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of Brutus and Cassius at odds. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene II within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Brutus and Cassius at odds responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Brutus and Cassius at odds follows or bends those conventions, using the conflict as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene II and its treatment of Brutus and Cassius at odds. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's conflict and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about Brutus and Cassius at odds in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Brutus and Cassius at odds. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

A hot friend cooling: ever note, Lucilius,
When love begins to sicken and decay,
It useth an enforced ceremony.

Make gallant show and promise of their mettle;
But when they should endure the bloody spur,
They fall their crests, and, like deceitful jades,
Sink in the trial. Comes his army on?
